focus: Exodus 3 brings Moses from the back of the desert into the presence of God at the burning bush, where the LORD reveals that He has seen His people’s suffering and has come down to deliver them through Moses. The chapter moves from the holy encounter to Moses’ commission, God’s promise and name, and detailed instructions that foresee Pharaoh’s resistance and Israel’s departure.

sections.title: The Angel of the LORD Appears in the Burning Bush
sections.summary: While tending Jethro’s flock at Horeb, Moses sees a bush burning with fire that “was not consumed” (Exodus 3:2) and turns aside to look. God calls him by name, declares the ground holy, and identifies Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and Moses hides his face in fear.

sections.title: The LORD Sends Moses with the Promise of His Presence
sections.summary: The LORD has seen the oppression of His people and heard their cry, and He has come down to deliver them and bring them to a good land, sending Moses to Pharaoh to bring them out. To Moses’ question “Who am I” (Exodus 3:11), God answers, “I will certainly be with you” (Exodus 3:12), and gives the sign that Israel will serve Him on this mountain.

sections.title: God Reveals His Name
sections.summary: When Moses asks what name to give the people, God answers, “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14), and sends Moses in the name of the LORD God of their fathers. He declares, “This is My name forever, and this is My memorial to all generations” (Exodus 3:15).

sections.title: God Foretells Israel’s Belief, Pharaoh’s Refusal, and the Departure
sections.summary: Moses is to gather the elders, tell them that the LORD has visited them, and go with them to ask Pharaoh to let Israel make a three days’ journey to sacrifice. God foretells that Pharaoh will refuse until God strikes Egypt with His wonders, and He promises Israel favor so that they will not leave empty-handed.

1.brief: Moses is tending the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian, when he leads it to the back of the desert and comes to Horeb, “the mountain of God.” In the middle of ordinary shepherd’s work, Moses arrives at the place where God will meet him.
1.explain:
“Now Moses was tending the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian.”

Moses, once a prince of Egypt, is now a shepherd. He “was tending the flock of Jethro his father-in-law.” The flock was not even his own. Jethro is the same man called Reuel in 2:18. Forty years have passed since Moses fled Egypt (Acts 7:30).

“And he led the flock to the back of the desert,”

The back of the desert means the far side of the wilderness, beyond the usual grazing areas. Shepherds moved their flocks in search of grass and water.

“and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.”

Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai, where God would later give the law (19:11; Deuteronomy 4:10, 15). Moses calls it “the mountain of God” because of what happened there. In the middle of ordinary shepherd’s work, Moses arrives at the place where God will meet him.
1.notes: The location of Mount Sinai is debated. The traditional site is Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula. Other proposed locations include sites in northwestern Arabia.

2.brief: The Angel of the LORD appears to Moses in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush, and the bush burns but “was not consumed.” The next verses identify the Angel as the LORD Himself, and His appearance here is best read as Christ before His incarnation.
2.explain:
“And the Angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush.”

“The Angel of the LORD appeared to him.” The word “Angel” means messenger, one sent. Yet as the scene unfolds, the One who appears is identified as the LORD Himself. In 3:4 “God called to him from the midst of the bush,” and in 3:6 He says, “I am the God of your father.” The Angel of the LORD speaks as God and is God. This appearance is best read as Christ before His incarnation, the Son making the Father known (John 1:18).

He appeared “in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush.” Fire often signals God’s presence in Scripture. It speaks of His holiness, His power, and His purifying judgment. Later God would lead Israel by a pillar of fire (13:21) and descend on Sinai in fire (19:18).

“So he looked, and behold, the bush was burning with fire, but the bush was not consumed.”

Moses “looked,” and what he saw was strange: “the bush was burning with fire, but the bush was not consumed.” A dry desert bush should have burned up quickly. This one kept burning without being destroyed. The fire did not depend on the bush for fuel. The holy God was present, drawing near without consuming the one He calls.
2.notes:
The Hebrew word for “bush” sounds similar to the name Sinai. The bush was most likely a thorny desert shrub.

The Angel of the LORD appears elsewhere in the Old Testament as One who speaks as God (for example, Genesis 16:7–13; 22:11–18; Judges 13:18–22).

3.brief: Moses decides to turn aside and see “this great sight, why the bush does not burn.” His curiosity draws him toward the place where God is about to speak.
3.explain:
“Then Moses said, ‘I will now turn aside and see this great sight, why the bush does not burn.”

Moses decided, “I will now turn aside.” He left his path and his flock to look closer. He wanted to understand “this great sight, why the bush does not burn.” His curiosity draws him toward the place where God is about to speak.

Moses could have ignored the bush and kept walking. He chose to stop and look. That small decision opened the way for the encounter that would change his life.

4.brief: When the LORD sees Moses turn aside, God calls to him from the midst of the bush, “Moses, Moses!” and Moses answers, “Here I am.” The God who drew Moses’ attention now calls him personally by name.
4.explain:
“So when the LORD saw that he turned aside to look,”

“When the LORD saw that he turned aside.” God watched Moses’ response. He waited until Moses turned aside before He spoke.

“God called to him from the midst of the bush and said, ‘Moses, Moses!”

“God called to him from the midst of the bush.” The speaker is now named “the LORD” and “God.” He called Moses by name, twice: “Moses, Moses!” Calling a name twice expressed urgency and closeness. God called Abraham the same way (Genesis 22:11), and later Samuel (1 Samuel 3:10).

“And he said, ‘Here I am.”

Moses answered, “Here I am.” It is the response of a servant ready to listen. The God who drew Moses’ attention now calls him personally by name.
4.notes: The verse uses both “the LORD” (the divine name YHWH) and “God,” showing that the Angel of 3:2 is the LORD Himself.

5.brief: God tells Moses not to come near and to take off his sandals, “for the place where you stand is holy ground.” The ground is holy because the holy God is present, and Moses must approach Him with reverence.
5.explain:
“Then He said, ‘Do not draw near this place.”

God’s first words set a boundary. “Do not draw near this place.” Moses had approached out of curiosity. Now he learns that he stands before the holy God. He cannot treat this as an interesting sight to examine.

“Take your sandals off your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground.”

“Take your sandals off your feet.” Removing sandals was a sign of reverence and humility. The reason is “the place where you stand is holy ground.” The ground was not holy in itself. It was holy because the holy God was present. Moses must approach Him with reverence.
5.notes:
Joshua received the same command from “the Commander of the LORD’s army” (Joshua 5:13–15).

This is the first use of the word “holy” in Exodus. Holiness will become a major theme in the book (for example, 15:11; 19:6; 28:36).

6.brief: God identifies Himself as the God of Moses’ father and the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and Moses hides his face, afraid to look upon God. The One speaking from the bush is the same God who made promises to the patriarchs.
6.explain:
“Moreover He said, ‘I am the God of your father—the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”

God identified Himself: “I am the God of your father.” He was the God Moses’ own father had worshiped. He is also “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” The One speaking from the bush is the same God who made promises to the patriarchs. He has not forgotten them.

Jesus later quoted this verse to show that the dead live before God: He is “not the God of the dead, but the God of the living” (Mark 12:26–27).

“And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look upon God.”

He understood that he stood in the presence of the holy God, and he was overwhelmed. Sinful people cannot look on God’s holiness casually.

7.brief: The LORD says, “I have surely seen the oppression of My people,” heard their cry, and knows their sorrows. He calls Israel “My people” and shows that their suffering has not escaped His notice.
7.explain:
“And the LORD said: ‘I have surely seen the oppression of My people who are in Egypt,”

“I have surely seen.” The Hebrew repeats the verb for emphasis: God has truly seen. He has seen “the oppression of My people.” God calls Israel “My people.” They belong to Him. Their suffering has not escaped His notice.

“and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters,”

God has heard what 2:23–24 described.

“for I know their sorrows.”

God does not merely observe from a distance. The word “know” speaks of personal, intimate knowledge. He knows their sorrows fully, and He cares about them as the grief of His own people.
7.notes: The verbs in 3:7 echo 2:24–25, where God heard, remembered, looked, and acknowledged. The LORD now tells Moses directly what the narrator described.

8.brief: The LORD says, “I have come down to deliver them” from the Egyptians and to bring them to a good and large land flowing with milk and honey. His purpose includes both rescue from Egypt and the gift of the land promised to the fathers.
8.explain:
“So I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians,”

“I have come down.” God does not stay distant. He comes down to act. His purpose is “to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians.” The God who sees and hears also rescues.

“and to bring them up from that land to a good and large land, to a land flowing with milk and honey,”

God’s purpose goes further than rescue. He will “bring them up from that land to a good and large land.” He will give them a home. The land is described as “flowing with milk and honey.” Milk came from flocks and herds grazing on rich pasture, and honey from bees among abundant flowers. The phrase pictures a fertile, abundant land.

“to the place of the Canaanites and the Hittites and the Amorites and the Perizzites and the Hivites and the Jebusites.”

The land is “the place of the Canaanites” and other peoples. God names the nations then living there. The land had been promised to Abraham’s descendants (Genesis 15:18–21). His purpose includes both rescue from Egypt and the gift of the land promised to the fathers.
8.notes: “A land flowing with milk and honey” appears here for the first time. It becomes the standard description of the promised land in the Pentateuch (for example, 3:17; 13:5; 33:3).

9.brief: The LORD repeats that the cry of Israel has reached Him and that He has seen how the Egyptians oppress them. The repetition presses home that God’s coming action is His answer to their cry.
9.explain:
“Now therefore, behold, the cry of the children of Israel has come to Me,”

God repeats what He has said. “The cry of the children of Israel has come to Me.” The repetition presses home that God’s coming action is His answer to their cry.

“and I have also seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them.”

God names the oppressors and their crime. Egypt will answer for what it has done.

10.brief: The LORD tells Moses, “I will send you to Pharaoh” to bring His people out of Egypt. The God who has come down to deliver chooses to act through Moses as His messenger.
10.explain:
“Come now, therefore, and I will send you to Pharaoh”

Then comes the call. The God who has come down to deliver chooses to act through Moses as His messenger. Moses will stand before Egypt’s king.

“that you may bring My people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt.”

Moses’ task is to “bring My people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt.” God calls them “My people” again. Forty years earlier Moses tried to deliver his people by his own hand and failed (2:11–15). Now God sends him with His authority.
10.notes: In 3:8 God says, “I have come down to deliver them.” In 3:10 He says, “I will send you.” God Himself is the deliverer, and Moses is His instrument.

11.brief: Moses answers, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh,” and bring Israel out of Egypt? The man who once tried to deliver his people in his own way now feels his inadequacy for the task.
11.explain:
“But Moses said to God, ‘Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh,”

Moses objected. “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?” He felt unworthy and unqualified. Forty years before, he had been confident enough to kill an Egyptian. Now, after years as a shepherd, he doubted himself.

“and that I should bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?”

He also doubted he could “bring the children of Israel out of Egypt.” The task seemed impossible. The man who once tried to deliver his people in his own way now felt his inadequacy for the task.

12.brief: God answers, “I will certainly be with you,” and gives a sign: when Moses has brought the people out, they will serve God on this mountain. The answer to Moses’ weakness is God’s own presence, and the goal of the rescue is worship.
12.explain:
“So He said, ‘I will certainly be with you.”

God did not answer Moses’ question by telling him who Moses was. He told Moses who would be with him: “I will certainly be with you.” The answer to Moses’ weakness is God’s own presence. Moses did not need to be adequate. God would be with him.

“And this shall be a sign to you that I have sent you:”

God gave “a sign” to confirm that He had sent Moses.

“When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain.”

The sign would come after Moses obeyed. Moses would have to trust God first, and the confirmation would follow. The goal of the rescue is worship. God would bring Israel to this same mountain to serve Him, which He did at Sinai (19:1–6).
12.notes:
The Hebrew words behind “I will certainly be with you” use the same verb “to be” that appears in God’s name in 3:14, “I AM.”

The verb translated “serve” is the same verb used for Israel’s forced labor in 1:13–14. Israel will move from serving Pharaoh to serving God.

13.brief: Moses asks what he should say when the people ask the name of the God who sent him. He wants to know how to make God known to Israel, and the question opens the revelation of God’s name.
13.explain:
“Then Moses said to God, ‘Indeed, when I come to the children of Israel and say to them, ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you,”

Moses raised another concern. When he goes to Israel and says “The God of your fathers has sent me to you,” they will ask a question.

“and they say to me, ‘What is His name?’ what shall I say to them?”

They will ask, “What is His name?” In the ancient world a name was more than a label. It revealed something of a person’s character. Israel would want to know who this God was and what He was like. Moses wants to know how to make God known to Israel, and the question opens the revelation of God’s name.

14.brief: God answers, “I AM WHO I AM,” and tells Moses to say, “I AM has sent me to you.” The name declares the God who exists in Himself and who is truly present with His people to deliver them.
14.explain:
“And God said to Moses, ‘I AM WHO I AM.”

God answered, “I AM WHO I AM.” This is God’s self-declaration. He is the God who exists in Himself. He depends on no one and nothing. He always has been and always will be. He is not defined by anything outside Himself.

The name also speaks of His faithful presence. God has just said, “I will certainly be with you” (3:12). The God who exists in Himself is also the God who is truly present with His people to deliver them.

“And He said, ‘Thus you shall say to the children of Israel, ‘I AM has sent me to you.”

Moses is to tell Israel, “I AM has sent me to you.” The self-existent God is the One sending Moses.

The name also answers a question: I am what? As Exodus unfolds, God shows what He is for His people. He is the LORD who heals (15:26), who provides (16:4), and who is Israel’s banner (17:15). Jesus took up this name when He said, “before Abraham was, I AM” (John 8:58). His “I am” sayings fill out the same name: “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35), “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).
14.notes: The Hebrew phrase translated “I AM WHO I AM” can also be translated I will be what I will be. The verb form allows both present and future meanings. The exact derivation of the divine name is debated.

15.brief: God adds that Moses is to call Him the LORD God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and declares, “This is My name forever, and this is My memorial to all generations.” The God of the patriarchs gives His name as a lasting way for His people to know and remember Him.
15.explain:
“Moreover God said to Moses, ‘Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘The LORD God of your fathers,”

God continued. Moses is to call Him “The LORD God of your fathers.” The name translated “LORD” (printed in small capitals in English Bibles) is the personal name of God, often written as YHWH. It is closely related to the verb “I AM” in 3:14. The God who said “I AM” is the LORD.

“the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.”

He is also “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” The personal name connects with God’s history with the patriarchs.

“This is My name forever, and this is My memorial to all generations.”

“This is My name forever.” God will always be known by this name. It is also “My memorial to all generations,” the way His people will remember Him. The God of the patriarchs gives His name as a lasting way for His people to know and remember Him.
15.notes: The divine name YHWH is printed “LORD” in the NKJV. Out of reverence, Jewish readers came to say “Lord” (Adonai) instead of pronouncing the name. The pronunciation “Yahweh” is a modern reconstruction.

16.brief: God tells Moses to gather the elders and tell them that the LORD God of their fathers appeared to him, saying, “I have surely visited you and seen what is done to you in Egypt.” The first audience for God’s message is Israel’s own leaders.
16.explain:
“Go and gather the elders of Israel together, and say to them,”

God gave Moses practical instructions. “Go and gather the elders of Israel together.” The “elders” were the leaders of the families and tribes. The first audience for God’s message is Israel’s own leaders.

“The LORD God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob, appeared to me, saying,”

Moses is to tell them that “The LORD God of your fathers” has “appeared to me.”

“I have surely visited you and seen what is done to you in Egypt;”

The message: “I have surely visited you.” To visit here means to come and pay attention, to act on behalf of someone. Joseph had promised, “God will surely visit you, and bring you out of this land” (Genesis 50:24). God is keeping that promise. He has “seen what is done to you in Egypt.”
16.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “visited” is the same verb Joseph used in Genesis 50:24–25.

17.brief: Moses is to tell them that God will bring them out of the affliction of Egypt to the land of the Canaanites and other peoples, “a land flowing with milk and honey.” God’s promise moves from rescue to inheritance.
17.explain:
“and I have said I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt”

God promises, “I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt.” The rescue is certain because God has said it.

“to the land of the Canaanites and the Hittites and the Amorites and the Perizzites and the Hivites and the Jebusites, to a land flowing with milk and honey.”

He will bring them “to the land of the Canaanites” and the other peoples, “a land flowing with milk and honey.” God’s promise moves from rescue to inheritance.
17.notes: This verse repeats the promise of 3:8 almost word for word, now as the message for the elders.

18.brief: God says the elders will heed Moses, and together they are to ask the king of Egypt to let Israel go three days’ journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to the LORD their God. The request centers on Israel’s freedom to worship their God.
18.explain:
“Then they will heed your voice;”

God assures Moses that the elders will listen. Moses’ fear in 4:1 that they will not believe him has already been answered here.

“and you shall come, you and the elders of Israel, to the king of Egypt;”

Moses and the elders together will go “to the king of Egypt.”

“and you shall say to him, ‘The LORD God of the Hebrews has met with us;”

They will tell Pharaoh, “The LORD God of the Hebrews has met with us.” They introduce their God by His relationship with the Hebrews.

“and now, please, let us go three days’ journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.”

The request is for a short journey to offer sacrifice. The request centers on Israel’s freedom to worship their God. It is a modest request that would test Pharaoh’s heart. If he would not allow even a short journey for worship, his opposition to God would be plain.
18.notes: Interpreters discuss whether the request for three days was meant as the full demand or as a first step. God’s later words make clear that His purpose was Israel’s complete release (3:8; 6:6–8). The modest request exposed Pharaoh’s refusal to let Israel worship God at all.

19.brief: God tells Moses that He knows the king of Egypt will not let them go, “no, not even by a mighty hand.” God prepares Moses in advance for Pharaoh’s stubborn refusal.
19.explain:
“But I am sure that the king of Egypt will not let you go, no, not even by a mighty hand.”

God prepared Moses for resistance. “I am sure that the king of Egypt will not let you go.” God knew Pharaoh would refuse. He would not yield “not even by a mighty hand,” unless he were forced by overwhelming power. God prepared Moses in advance for Pharaoh’s stubborn refusal.
19.notes: The phrase “not even by a mighty hand” can also be translated unless by a mighty hand, and the Greek translation reads that way. Either way, Pharaoh will yield only to God’s power.

20.brief: God declares that He will stretch out His hand and strike Egypt with all His wonders, “and after that he will let you go.” Pharaoh’s resistance will be overcome by God’s own power.
20.explain:
“So I will stretch out My hand and strike Egypt with all My wonders which I will do in its midst;”

God will act. “I will stretch out My hand.” God’s hand stands for His power. He will “strike Egypt with all My wonders.” The “wonders” are the miraculous judgments, the plagues, that God will bring on Egypt.

“and after that he will let you go.”

Pharaoh’s resistance will be overcome by God’s own power. What Pharaoh refuses at first, he will be forced to grant.

21.brief: God promises to give Israel favor with the Egyptians, so that when they go, “you shall not go empty-handed.” The God who rescues His people will also provide for them as they leave.
21.explain:
“And I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians;”

God promises to change the Egyptians’ attitude toward Israel. The same Egyptians who oppressed Israel will be moved to show them kindness.

“and it shall be, when you go, that you shall not go empty-handed.”

“when you go, that you shall not go empty-handed.” Israel will not leave as poor runaway slaves. They will leave with possessions. The God who rescues His people will also provide for them as they leave.

22.brief: Every woman is to ask her neighbor for articles of silver, gold, and clothing to put on their sons and daughters, and so Israel will plunder the Egyptians. The Egyptians will give these things in response to Israel’s request, as God promised Abraham that his descendants would come out with great possessions.
22.explain:
“But every woman shall ask of her neighbor, namely, of her who dwells near her house, articles of silver, articles of gold, and clothing;”

God gave instructions. “Every woman shall ask of her neighbor.” The Israelite women would ask the Egyptian women living near them for “articles of silver, articles of gold, and clothing.” The word “ask” means to request.

“and you shall put them on your sons and on your daughters.”

These gifts would be put “on your sons and on your daughters.” Israel’s children would wear what Egypt gave.

“So you shall plunder the Egyptians.”

The word “plunder” usually describes taking spoil after a victory. Here the Egyptians will give these things willingly in response to Israel’s request (12:35–36). God will give Israel the spoil of a victory won by His hand alone. This also fulfilled God’s promise to Abraham that his descendants would come out “with great possessions” (Genesis 15:14), and it served as partial recompense for generations of unpaid labor. It gives no precedent for taking from others.
22.notes:
Exodus 12:35–36 records the fulfillment: “the LORD had given the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they granted them what they requested. Thus they plundered the Egyptians.”

Exodus 35:22 records men and women bringing earrings, nose rings, rings, necklaces, and jewelry of gold for the tabernacle. That verse does not say where the individual articles came from. Some may have been among the things Israel received from the Egyptians, but Exodus gives no such inventory.
